#5564. Police Raid $4.4 Million San Francisco Squatter Mansion—Arresting Woman and Rescuing 7 Dogs

The woman allegedly at the center of a squatting dispute in San Francisco’s luxury Sea Cliff community was arrested on Friday during a raid of the property and following a monthslong investigation into her claims on the home. Diana Peng, 42, was charged with fraud, driving without a license, narcotics possession, improper care of animals, and being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition. Police also removed seven dogs from the home and put them in the care of a local shelter.

Peng and her alleged accomplice, Brandon Aadee, are in the midst of a civil lawsuit brought by San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu. Chiu accused the pair of illegally obtaining the $4.4 million property through forged, fraudulently notarized deeds, intending to sell it.

According to Chiu’s complaint, Peng and Aadee took over the 3,000-square-foot Tudor-style home at 250 32nd Ave. in 2025 by claiming that the previous owner had transferred the deed to Aadee. Peng and Aadee transferred the property title back and forth between them eight times, and at least five of those were forged, including the initial deed from the legitimate owner, Wei Wang, which includes a forged notary signature.

Wang and her husband, Xiangdong Guo, purchased the property in 2013 for $2.41 million. But the pair moved abroad around 2019, and the property fell into disrepair and appeared to be abandoned.

It also racked up more than $340,000 in unpaid property taxes, which prevented a sale of the property.

This past October, however, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to pay off the property taxes, paving the way for the home to be put up for auction later this year.

Neighbors in the wealthy enclave, where both Sharon Stone and Twitter founder Jack Dorsey have homes, said they spent much of the past year on edge, watching people come and go from the property at all hours.

"I'm probably in touch with one city official or another at least six times every day," neighbor Whitney Lynn told ABC 7. "We really have been asking for help, and it feels like people finally heard us.Most recently, in August, a neighbor called 311 to complain that the property was “being used as a group home.”

“The home was abandoned for over 5 years, and squatters moved in May 2025 using burglary tools. Over the past couple of days, a new group of about a dozen squatters moved in," the complaint read. Nearly a dozen complaints were also filed with the Department of Building Inspection, the most recent on Oct. 13. That complaint stated that unpermitted plumbing and irrigation work had been taking place in the backyard.

Neighbors told the San Francisco Chronicle that Friday’s raid lasted about four hours and that police removed several boxes and bags of documents. Police went in with guns drawn and came out with Peng, and seven dogs were removed from the property and taken to a local shelter. Police also towed Peng's Porsche.

Deb Campbell, the public information officer with San Francisco Animal Care and Control, tells Realtor.com® the two adult pit bulls and five puppies are “doing well in our care.” She otherwise couldn’t comment on the animals' condition because of the ongoing investigation.

“We appreciate SFPD’s work to pursue accountability and keep our neighborhoods safe,” Jen Kwart, the communications director for the city attorney’s office, tells Realtor.com. "As our civil case moves forward, we look forward to continuing to work closely with SFPD to ensure the courts understand that Defendants are effectively trying to steal a house and sell it to make millions in profit.”

Both Peng and Aadee have long criminal records. In 2008, she was convicted of perjury and sentenced to 90 days in jail and three years’ probation. Four years later, she pleaded guilty to identity theft and burglary and served seven months in prison. And then in 2015, she was sentenced to an additional two years in jail for forgery of a driver’s license and using another person's identification.

In 2009, Aadee was convicted of defrauding FEMA out of thousands of dollars and ordered to pay $48,000 in restitution. He also has convictions for credit card fraud and passing bad checks.

Following Friday’s raid, Peng was booked and is being held without bail at the San Francisco County Jail.

#5563. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

#5561. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5560. The 5 Biggest Mistakes Veteran and Military Homebuyers Make

Having a place to call your own—whether it's your starter home or your forever home—is an essential part of the American dream. And the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs offers plenty of great programs to help those who have served in the military become first-time homebuyers.

However, the process to get a home loan as a veteran isn’t foolproof.

"Being eligible for a VA loan and ultimately able to secure one are different things," explains Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight and education at Veterans United Home Loans. "Prospective buyers will still need to meet credit, income, and other guidelines set by both the VA and by the lenders that make these loans."

You can set yourself up for success before you even start your home search and avoid making missteps that have held other prospective homebuyers back.

We asked VA-savvy real estate agents to tell us which missteps they see the most—and how you can avoid them when you apply for and get a VA loan.

If you’re getting a VA loan, make sure you work with a real estate agent who understands the VA home loan process.

“The VA won’t underwrite [just] any house," says Katie Fraser, a Realtor® with Keller Williams Tacoma. "It is a huge, huge, huge deal to use an agent who understands the VA home loan system, the VA appraisal process, and what that all really looks like.”

When you’re buying through the Veterans Affairs Department, you’ll need to find a home that meets VA home loan property requirements. A VA loan program appraiser will have specific criteria. An agent experienced with home loans for veterans will also know about VA loan limits, the debt-to-income ratio lenders will expect you to have to qualify for a home loan, and other essential information.

So, save yourself the heartache of making an offer on a house that may not get approved, or for which you may not qualify for a VA loan, and work with a VA-experienced real estate agent from the start. Ask another veteran for a referral, or get help from Veterans United Realty to find the right real estate agent.

Veterans have access to arguably the most powerful home mortgage option on the market, yet still far too many veterans don’t know about VA loans.

When you first talk with your lender, be sure to discuss your service history so you can be informed about all of the potential advantages for veterans.

One of the biggest benefits you’ll get with a VA loan is the ability to buy with a 0% down payment (yes, we're totally serious). Not having to make a down payment can make it possible for veterans  to buy a first home, often years sooner than if they had to save up for a down payment first.

VA loans also come with low-interest-rate mortgages, don't require private mortgage insurance, and have more forgiving credit eligibility requirements.

"Veterans should ask their lender if they offer any incentives for veterans," adds Alissa Gerke, broker and owner of Select Realty Group in Columbia, MO. "I’ve seen lenders waive appraisal fees, offer a waiver of origination fee if the veteran has a certain credit score, or other lender credits."

Pretty much everything will get easier as soon as your lender knows you're a veteran or service member, so speak up!

While you'll have a ton of financial advantages with your VA loan, you will have some borrower costs to deal with.

“Probably the biggest mistake I see is active-duty members coming into the homebuying process and not knowing there are other closing costs and fees necessary for buying a home,” Fraser says.

When you’re buying a home, even if you have little or no down payment, you’ll likely have to plunk down a bit of cash for things like a home appraisal and inspection. It might not cost much in the large scheme of things, but it'll help speed things along if you come prepared knowing what you'll have to shell out for.

Maybe you think there's no sense in buying if there's a chance you might be relocated in the next few years. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't buy. In fact, that home could end up being a smart investment.

By searching in high-demand areas or choosing a popular home style and size (say, 1,500 to 2,000 square feet), you’ll give yourself a better chance at resale if you need to move later. Or, you can hang on to it and rent it out.

My clients and I "often go out and look for their first rental home, not just a home for their family," Fraser says. "With so many in transition, they’re able to purchase a home and it becomes an investment property for them when they go on to their next duty station or they move.”

Don’t like the idea of becoming a landlord? A VA loan is assumable (meaning you can transfer the loan and the property to another person), or you can just sell the home and regain your full VA loan entitlement.

Don’t forget: You can use your VA home loan benefits again and again, so you can own a rental property and a new home. You can even refinance a VA loan if you are an active-duty service member. You may want to refinance if you have a non-VA loan, want to increase your loan amount and tap into your home equity, or want to get a better interest rate with a new VA loan.

Once homebuyers find a home and their offer is accepted, they can be excited about moving in and making it theirs. Maybe you have an eye on a new big-screen TV, and you're looking into financing a new living room set you love. But don’t do that until you're really a homeowner, even if your lender has approved your mortgage loan.

It's easier to get a VA loan than a conventional, non-VA loan, but you still must meet lender requirements.

“Opening a line of credit or making a big purchase after mortgage approval is a common mistake,” Gerke says. “This can oftentimes change the veteran's credit score and make them ineligible for the loan.”

Wait until after closing to make any other financial moves, just to be on the safe side and to keep your loan on track.

Angela Colley writes about real estate and all things renting and moving for Realtor.com. Her work has appeared in outlets including TheStreet, MSN, and Yahoo.

#5559. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5558. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5557. NAR Board Approves 2027 Budget, Installs New Leadership

At its Nov. 9 meeting during NAR NXT in New Orleans, the National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) board of directors approved a 2027 budget and installed new leadership.

The board approved an operating budget projecting approximately $280 million in revenue and $247 million in expenses. Under the new approach, NAR departments were required to evaluate expenditures from the ground up rather than simply carry forward previous spending levels, prioritizing initiatives and identifying measures of success.

NAR Treasurer Craig Sanford described the approach as a significant step in the association’s financial modernization efforts. The board approved the budget by an overwhelming majority.

Directors also approved the following financial recommendations:

In his final board of directors meeting as NAR president, Kevin Brown highlighted progress on initiatives aimed at protecting members’ business interests, expanding housing opportunities and helping members adapt to a changing industry.

He also highlighted progress on MLS collaboration, including outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives and the formation of a work group to address emerging challenges and modernize policies. That work helped inform four policy recommendations approved by NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR NXT, aimed at strengthening copyright protections for listing content, giving MLSs greater flexibility in setting local data feed requirements and clarifying permitted uses of MLS data.

For Realtor® members, the changes address business concerns, including protecting the time and money invested in marketing properties, preserving access to their own listing information and establishing clearer rules for how listing data can be used and shared.

Brown also pointed to NAR’s advocacy surrounding the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a housing package aimed at increasing supply, improving affordability and expanding homeownership opportunities. NAR’s attention is now turning toward implementation, including working with federal agencies and supporting state and local associations.

Other initiatives highlighted during the meeting included six “modernized” Center for REALTOR® Development courses scheduled to launch Dec. 1, more broker summits (on track for 85-plus by the end of the year) and continued advocacy, including for the bipartisan More Homes on the Market Act, which would increase the capital gains tax exclusion for homeowners selling their primary residences (something the Trump administration previously floated as well).

New NAR President Christine E. Hansen’s priorities include advancing NAR’s three-year strategic plan, improving awareness of member tools and resources, and restoring pride in the Realtor® brand.

The association’s 13 regional vice presidents were also installed.

#5556. AMD brings Zen 6 architecture muscle to embedded systems with new EPYC 9006 series chips

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. is delivering a massive compute upgrade to the specialized embedded systems used to validate semiconductor technologies with the launch of its 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Series SP7 processors.

Announced today, the new chips are designed to bring superior performance to semiconductor automated test equipment or ATE, enterprise storage systems and high-end network firewalls, the company said.

AMD is targeting what it says is mounting friction in the semiconductor hardware supply chain with its new processors. As the data demands of artificial intelligence workloads increase, the systems used to validate, secure and move that data are reaching their limits.

Semiconductor ATE workloads in particular are showing signs of strain. They’re performed by automated testing rigs that act as high-speed quality control during chip manufacturing operations, running continuous electrical parametric tests, functional stress tests and signal validation across dozens of silicon dies simultaneously.

The goal of these tests is to identify any defects or performance issues with new silicon chips before they reach mass production, but as their performance capabilities increase, existing ATE controllers are unable to provide the massive parallel compute power required to orchestrate them.

AMD’s EPYC Embedded 9006 family is designed to eliminate this bottleneck. It’s based on the company’s high-performance Zen 6 core architecture and it packs up to 256 cores and 512 threads into a single socket. It’s an extremely dense computing footprint that delivers 1.8 times more throughput, 1.5 times greater networking bandwidth and 2.7 times higher memory bandwidth than the company’s previous 5th Generation 9005 series embedded chips.

They can also facilitate much more rapid data movement with up to 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6 running at 64 gigatransfers per second, with flexible CXL 3.1 expansion and 16 DDR5 memory channels that support multiplexed rank dual inline memory module speeds of up to 12,800 megatransfers per second. That last number refers to the chip’s effective data transfer rate between the memory controller and the memory module, and represents a significant jump from the standard 6,400 to 8,000 MT/s of standard, high-end server DDR5 random-access memory chips.

AMD said EPYC Embedded 9006 series chips can also provide more control plane muscle for 400G and 800G network firewalls. that enables them to process expanding security policies better, as well as faster compression and redundant array of independent disks in storage workloads.

Salil Raje, senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s Adaptive and Embedded Computing Group, said the industry urgently needs this increased computing heft at the embedded layer if it’s to maintain the momentum of its current development cadence. “The systems that test semiconductors, secure networks and manage enterprise data must keep pace or risk becoming bottlenecks to progress,” he said. “With AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 SP7 processors, we’re extending AMD CPU leadership by bringing data center-class compute to embedded systems and by helping customers increase capacity and do more within their power budgets.”

When it comes to testing advanced semiconductor designs, security is of paramount importance, and that’s why AMD introduced a number of innovations on that front. For instance, the EPYC Embedded 9006 chips incorporate the company’s Root of Trust or ART technology to establish an immutable boot chain, secured by post-quantum cryptography, to safeguard firmware signing against potential threats from quantum computers in the future.

There’s also a new AMD Security Processor or ASP that handles runtime trust execution, virtual machine encryption and authorized diagnostic debugging. The chips further integrate Caliptra, which is an open-source and vendor-agnostic silicon root of trust technology that supports remote attestation to mathematically verify device identities and prevent firmware tampering.

With mass volume production already underway, the 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Series SP7 processors are expected to be shipped to customers later this month, the company said. Customers will be able to choose from configurations ranging from 64 to 256 cores, with the first 128-core offering launching on Nov. 15.

#5555. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5554. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

#5553. Billy Joel Is Returning to the Stage—Months After Selling His Long Island Estate and Revealing Brain Disorder

Billy Joel is returning to performing—months after he offloaded his Long Island estate and nearly one year after revealing a brain disorder diagnosis.

The hitmaker, 77, revealed in a Nov. 9 social media post that he would be making his on-stage comeback.

“Florida Atlantic University will welcome singer, songwriter, and composer Billy Joel for Billy Joel: An Evening of Questions & Answers…And a Little Music,” he penned on Instagram, alongside a snap of himself singing.

The post revealed that he would be performing on Dec. 14, adding that tickets would be exclusively available to currently enrolled students at FAU.

This will mark Joel's first official performance since he announced on May 23 that he would be calling off his tour in order to focus on treatment for normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)—which occurs when there's a buildup of fluid in the brain, causing difficulty walking and balancing, confusion, and forgetfulness, per the Cleveland Clinic.

According to a statement released by the singer's spokesperson on Instagram, his condition has been "exacerbated by recent concert performances, leading to problems with hearing, vision, and balance," forcing him to bow out of his planned tour dates.

“Under his doctor’s instructions, Billy is undergoing specific physical therapy and has been advised to refrain from performing during this recovery period. Billy is thankful for the excellent care he is receiving and is fully committed to prioritizing his health," the announcement continued.

The statement added that the "Piano Man" singer was thankful for his fans' "support" and that he "looks forward" to performing when his health is in a better place.

"I'm sincerely sorry to disappoint our audience, and thank you for your understanding," Joel added in a quote.

At the end of the statement, fans were reassured that they won't need to take any action to receive their refunds, adding that their payments will be automatically refunded to the original form of payment.

The concert dates that were affected by the news include shows in New York City; New Orleans; Toronto; Santa Clara, CA; Salt Lake City; Washington, D.C., and Liverpool.

Months after he announced his diagnosis, his daughter, Alexa, gave fans a long-awaited update on her dad's performance schedule, telling the Hollywood Reporter that he is a "trooper."

She noted that her father was looking forward to returning to Carnegie Hall on March 19, where his daughter will be belting out his hits at a tribute event.

Alexa explained, “I said, ‘Dad, you better be there! This is Carnegie Hall. Everyone’s paying tribute to you, and it’s an amazing group of artists.' He was like, ‘Let me mark that down.’ He’s very organized with his little calendar. He was so excited when he first played Carnegie Hall in the ‘70s, so it’s exciting for him to come back decades later and see amazing artists and his daughter pay tribute to him. It’s a full-circle moment."

The 40-year-old singer-songwriter also noted that her father's health is much better.

"He’s doing physical therapy regularly, and he’s doing great," she revealed. "He’s lost weight as he’s on his diet. I’m so proud of him. He’s such a trooper, so resilient and committed to being healthy and proactive. He’s a fighter. He’s always been a fighter and talks in his documentary about how life’s like a fight.”

She added, "He played it down. He knows I have anxiety and am a neurotic worrier, so he was, like, ‘Everything’s fine. It was just a little trip.’ When I saw the footage, I was crying. But then I went with him to the doctors, and we’re on top of everything. I just tell him to stay healthy.”

“Once a performer, always a performer! But health comes first. I said, ‘If you’re going to perform again, please stay seated at the piano. No throwing the microphone stand around!’" she revealed.

Alexa's update on her father's health came mere weeks after he finally offloaded his Long Island estate.

Joel had been trying to sell a large portion of his Long Island estate since March 2025, when it was listed for $39.9 million, having initially put the entirety of the property, which is made up of three parcels, on the market for the even higher price of $49 million.

However, after months with no concrete offers, the asking price of the property's main residence was slashed, first to $29.9 million, then to $25 million.

In 2025, he sold the seven-bedroom, nine-bathroom gatehouse for $7 million. On March 6, 2026, Billy sold the main property—dubbed "Middlesea"—for $23.2 million, as well as a pair of adjoining lots that brought the total to $35.75 million.

He purchased his Long Island sanctuary in 2002 for $22.5 million before picking up two adjoining plots.

The main residence, which comes with 14.6 acres, was formerly on the market for $25 million, while the two adjacent plots were listed for $3.5 million each.

When deciding to separate the areas, Emmett Laffey, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Laffey International Realty, said, "The new price reflects the splitting of the two buildable waterfront lots, so the gross price remains the same."

“When [Billy Joel] bought this 20 years ago, he bought the main house. And then as he lived there, he bought the adjacent two lots, which are buildable lots, and he purchased a gatehouse. Now we’re selling it like he bought it—in pieces. The smartest way to sell this incredible land and property is the way he purchased it," Laffey previously told the Post.

Laffey noted that many super "fans" have already attempted to snap up the property and have put in several offers.

“You do have some extreme fans. It is very special. It’s a very famous home to everyone on the North Shore of Long Island," he said.

The main house sprawls over 20,000 square feet and comes with five bedrooms, six full baths, two half-baths, a playroom, a spa and hair salon, a bowling alley, and a wine cellar.

There's also an indoor pool, which Billy had covered up so he could use the space as a music room, because of its excellent acoustics.

The estate also features a three-bedroom beach house, a three-bedroom guest apartment, and a four-bedroom gatehouse, which has since been sold.

Other luxe amenities include a floating dock and boat ramp, two outdoor pools, and a helipad.

Billy previously insisted that he would still call Long Island home, but would be spending more time in Florida.

Although Billy and Alexa tend to focus on music, they have previously exchanged real estate, with him having sold his Manhattan property, a two-bedroom condo, for $4.5 million to Alexa.

Despite passing the dwelling to his own family member, the singer didn't hold back with the price, earning an impressive $1.2 million profit on the $3.3 million he paid for the Elizabeth Street dwelling in 2010, when he purchased it from his then-wife, Katie Lee.

Property records now reveal that the two-bedroom, two-bathroom dwelling has been transferred to Alexa following a $4.5 million transaction, as first reported by Crain's.

The home, which sits at 211 Elizabeth St., spans 1,600 square feet. Pre-staged photos revealed dark herringbone floors, black crown moldings, and a dark-toned chef's kitchen, according to Curbed.

Transferring the property into his daughter's name was a formality for the most part, as it has been reported that Alexa has been living in the dwelling since 2010.

#5552. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5551. The 2027 Paint Colors of the Year Take an Emotional Turn

In the past, one hue typically dominated paint colors of the year, with different brands interpreting the color. For 2027, while there are a few blues and greens on offer, there is a much wider variety. Themes are less color-specific and more about emotional intent.

“Color has always been tied to emotion. We instinctively use it to create spaces that make us feel a certain way, and the colors we choose often reflect what we’re looking for in our lives,” says Lisbeth Parada, color marketing manager for Dutch Boy and Minwax brands.

​In 2027, that’s digital detox, permission to be authentic, and the opportunity for stillness and reflection.

​“We’re living in a world increasingly shaped by technology, algorithms, and an almost constant stream of information telling us what to think, what to buy, and how to live. We sense a growing desire to reconnect with our own instincts and the tangible experiences that make us feel human,” says Phillipa Radon, interior designer and C2 paint color specialist.

This year’s color trends tell us it’s not enough to treat home as a retreat anymore; recharging is necessary too, to manage the fast pace of the world around us. The variety of colors suggests multiple ways to gather that energy, with consumers choosing what resonates with them.

In new-construction homes, color choice is even more important, with paint offering homeowners a powerful way to personalize a brand-new space and forge that emotional connection to restoration.

​Here are the paint colors of the year for 2027.

​Sometimes paint color names are intentionally vague as part of their marketing micro-story. Not BEHR’s Grounded, with a name and a mossy green color that instantly frame the experience.

Its name has a double meaning too, as an invitation to breathe and get back to basics, amid digital overwhelm.

“What makes Grounded so relevant as BEHR’s 2027 Color of the Year is the way it balances two things people increasingly want from their homes: calm, and a feeling of life,” says Kayla Kratz, head of color at BEHR.

She notes that for many years, that meant paring down to a minimalist aesthetic, but today’s homeowners want more warmth and personality.

“Grounded answers that shift. The moss and olive tones bring a natural vitality, while warm brown undertones add depth and steadiness. The result is restorative without being static.”

Kratz says that the color replicates the dynamic greens of a forest, evolving throughout the day and changing light conditions.

​Deep Rooted, a nature-inspired warm orange, is energetic but steady and reassuring.

​“There’s an optimistic quality to the color. It has enough richness and energy to support bold contrasts and individual expression. The name brings those ideas together: feeling rooted while remaining open to possibility, and Deep Rooted captures that balance,” says Parada.

​It’s a perfect example of how paint color names are shaping the experience this year, with this color meant to encourage strength by standing still, not always easily done in today’s fast pace of living.

“​The paint color name captures both the color’s connection to nature and the sense of grounding many people want their homes to provide. At home, that translates into spaces that feel personal, welcoming, and comfortably lived in,” says Parada.

​Artifact is a smoky, atmospheric blue intended to create space to pause, recalibrate, and think more clearly after you’ve had a chance to catch your breath. These moments in time are both treasured and rare, which is reflected in the paint color name.

Artifact also embraces the idea of authorship, and how major change doesn’t necessarily require a makeover.

​“As consumers move away from creating homes that look like everyone else’s, they’re focusing on spaces that reflect who they are, where they’ve been, and what matters most to them, “ says Ashley McCollum, color marketing manager at Glidden.

​“People don’t necessarily want to reinvent themselves or start from scratch but rather make thoughtful adjustments that help their life feel more balanced and manageable,” says McCollum.

​“Artifact is not a reinvention, but a readjustment. It brings a sense of ease and relaxation after a busy day, helping you to unwind and feel more grounded. As a mid-tone, smoky blue, it leans warmer and has depth that strikes a balance between focus and comfort.”

This calming blue is nuanced and versatile, the kind of color that’s felt before it is seen, making it a good choice for homeowners who are choosing colors for an emotional impact.

Celery is a light green with yellow undertones that feels more herbal than botanical. It’s fresh and lively, marking a transition for Sherwin-Williams’ color trends.

Their paint color of the year last year was Universal Khaki, inspired by nostalgia and the comfort found in familiarity. Celery takes that feel-good energy into the future on a positive note. The color emerges alongside consumers’ appetite for expressive colors and a continued focus on wellness design.

A few paint colors of the year for 2027 are green, a carryover from last year’s color trends, but Celery offers a different perspective.

“While deeper, earthier greens have helped create grounded, restorative spaces, we’re beginning to see that nature-inspired palette evolve in a more expressive and optimistic direction,” says Ashley Banbury, color market manager at Sherwin-Williams.

“Celery reflects this shift, bringing a lighter, more playful energy to a color family that homeowners already know and love. It shows that green can be both calming and invigorating, offering a fresh perspective on nature-inspired design while encouraging homeowners to embrace color in more personal and unexpected ways,” says Banbury.

C2’s Pueblo is one of the more dynamic colors this year, with its identity shaped by an intentional refusal to commit to a single hue.

“What makes Pueblo so fascinating is that it resists a single definition. At its heart, it’s a warm, muted rose that bridges the space between deep floral tones and earthy neutrals. Its nuanced undertones interact with the changing temperature and intensity of natural light, revealing different aspects of the color throughout the day,” says Radon.

​“That complexity brings an unusual sense of dimension to an interior. Rather than creating a static backdrop, Pueblo becomes part of the experience of living in a space.”

​In the context of this year’s color themes, Pueblo taps into the idea that creativity and movement create energy to digitally detox.

​“There’s a certain confidence in choosing a color like that. It suggests we’re ready to move beyond simply creating a sanctuary and begin using our homes as places for creativity, individuality, and renewed engagement with life,” Radon says.

​Benjamin Moore has gone all-in on timeless over trends this year with their choice of Webster Green, a classic forest green that the paint brand is betting has staying power, given how prevalent various shades of green have been in color trends over the last few years.

​Green is adaptable and inherently energizing, which makes this shade a relevant tool for homeowners who want something sturdy but stylish too. Timeless design and decor choices are becoming more important to homeowners, for the sake of affordability and sustainability too.

​“Webster Green reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected, and continually new,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, at Benjamin Moore.​

​A sultry brown with plum undertones, French Press Coffee is all about striking the right mood and elevating daily rituals, another approach to gathering energy ahead of the daily grind. It’s the color equivalent to providing time and space to savor a hot, highly flavorful cup of coffee.

​It’s a little more nuanced than some of the other moody hues released in years prior, thanks to multidimensional color that adds visual weight and interest, while broadening potential applications.

​”French Press Coffee is the kind of color that reveals itself gradually,” said Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards. “As light shifts throughout the day, its subtle plum undertone emerges, adding complexity you don’t always see in a neutral. It’s grounding and restrained yet full of character.”

Blues dominated 2023’s colors of the year for their spa-inspired calm, and Valspar is rekindling those vibes. Chosen for being familiar but fresh, Cottage Door is a mid-toned blue with warm undertones.

Sue Kim, director of color marketing at Valspar, says that the color, “is reflective and warm, with timeless appeal that feels personal and grounding. Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortlessly into the home. It creates spaces that feel balanced, comforting, and inviting.”

The color taps into consumers’ increasingly pragmatic view on home design, and the company touts it as “designed for real life.” Homeowners would rather choose a color that endures than redecorate tomorrow.

#5550. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5549. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5548. How Buyers Can Tell if a Home Price Cut Signals a True Deal

More than one in five U.S. home listings received a price cut in August, but a lower asking price does not necessarily mean the property has become a good deal. Price reductions are becoming harder for homebuyers to ignore. In August, 20.4% of U.S. listings had a price cut, matching the rate recorded a year earlier, according to the latest Realtor.com housing report.

The median asking price fell 1.3% year over year to $424,500, marking the tenth consecutive month of annual declines. Meanwhile, pending sales slipped 0.2%, ending an eight-month run of year-over-year growth.

For buyers, the growing number of reductions may look like an invitation to start bargain hunting. However, a crossed-out asking price provides little evidence of the property’s actual value.

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says Jeremy Olsher, a principal at Mizner Residential Group. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.”

Olsher recommends three checks before treating a reduced listing as a deal.

Compare the new price with completed sales. Buyers should begin with recently sold properties that are genuinely comparable in location, size, condition and features. Active listings reveal what other sellers hope to receive, while completed sales show what buyers have accepted.

A $40,000 reduction may look substantial, but it has limited meaning if the home remains $50,000 above comparable sales.

“The percentage reduction is the part buyers notice first because it is easy to understand,” Olsher says. “The more useful question is whether the new price makes sense beside the homes that have actually sold.”

Read the entire listing history. The number and timing of reductions can reveal how the seller is responding to the market. A single adjustment after several quiet weeks may indicate growing flexibility. Several small reductions can suggest the seller is chasing the market downward without fully accepting current buyer demand.

Buyers should also check whether the home was previously listed, withdrawn and returned with a new price or description. A fresh listing date does not always mean the property is new to the market.

“Days on the market need context,” Olsher says. “I want to know whether the seller made one meaningful correction or has spent months making small changes that never addressed the real pricing problem.”

Account for condition and ownership costs. A reduced property can remain expensive once repairs, insurance, taxes, association fees and immediate maintenance are considered. Buyers should compare the home’s total financial exposure with competing properties, rather than evaluating the asking price in isolation.

A lower price may represent genuine value when the cost of resolving known issues has already been reflected. It becomes less attractive when the discount is smaller than the work or ongoing expenses the buyer will inherit.

There may also be room to offer below the revised price, particularly when comparable sales support a lower figure or the property has remained available after multiple reductions. Olsher advises buyers to base that offer on evidence rather than choosing an arbitrary percentage below asking.

“The strongest offer is not necessarily the closest to the seller’s latest number,” he says. “It is the one a buyer can explain with recent sales, property condition and realistic costs. A reduction opens the conversation. The numbers still have to hold up.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5547. NYC Property Transfers Show Growing Warning Signs of Deed Theft

More than one-third of New York City transfers of one- to three-family homes from individual owners to companies last year had gaps in their ownership records that researchers say could signal deed theft or other predatory schemes.

The findings come just days after Victor Quimis, 40, became the first person convicted under New York's criminal deed theft law, after admitting to stealing the home of an elderly Queens widow who was receiving hospice care.

Quimis and an accomplice forged Renuka Bherwani's signature to transfer ownership of the Kew Gardens Hills home she had owned for decades, according to prosecutors—first to themselves and then to a corporation controlled by Quimis.

He subsequently obtained a $552,500 mortgage against the property, pocketing more than $300,000 after paying off existing debts. Bherwani's family discovered the theft only after receiving a city notice congratulating Quimis on becoming the home's new owner.

“My mother lived in that house for nearly 40 years, and she was in hospice care in it when her home was stolen out from under her," said Kamal Bherwani, Renuka’s son and the executor of her estate. “Deed theft targets the elderly and the vulnerable, and I urge any family that sees something wrong with a deed to call the Attorney General's Office immediately."

Researchers at New York University's Furman Center are now seeking to better detect potential fraud through patterns in public ownership records, too.

Their latest analysis found that 34.5% of transfers from individual homeowners to companies in 2025 involved a mismatch between the seller on the new deed and the buyer on the previous deed—the highest share in at least a decade.

The share of transactions with mismatched ownership records has climbed from 26.8% in 2021, while an additional 1.4% of transfers in 2025 involved properties with no previous deed on record.

While these discrepancies don’t necessarily indicate fraud—they can also arise through legitimate transactions like foreclosures—researchers say they can help identify properties warranting closer scrutiny.

In New York City, that scrutiny is particularly important. Decades of rising property values have left longtime homeowners and their heirs with a huge amount of wealth that could be vulnerable to exploitation.

Earlier research from the center identified approximately 45,000 homes worth a combined $34.7 billion with at least one indicator of vulnerability to title-related problems or predatory tactics.

The latest report narrows its focus to 2,300 properties at particularly high risk because at least one listed owner is deceased and the property has no recorded deed or one dating back more than 30 years.

That can create difficulties for heirs from establishing their legal rights to the house—an issue that can compound by cutting off access to home equity or financial assistance, or even create difficulties paying necessary bills.

Indeed, nearly 13% of these high-risk properties owed more than $500 in property taxes, compared with fewer than 2% of all individually owned one- to three-family homes. And they were nearly seven times as likely to have appeared on the city's 2025 tax lien sale list.

The findings come as New York City expands efforts to combat deed theft. In April, Mayor Zohran Mamdani established the Mayor's Office of Deed Theft Prevention to coordinate investigations and protections for vulnerable homeowners.

“This is exactly the kind of crime the state's new anti-deed theft law is intended to deter," Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. said in a statement following Quimis' plea. "Queens homeowners can sleep better knowing our Attorney General will be aggressive in using this anti-deed theft law to protect the homes they have worked so hard for.”

The borough accounted for more than half of the city's high-risk properties, according to NYU's latest research. Meanwhile, the Bronx had the highest prevalence relative to its housing stock.

Jamaica and Hollis in Queens also recorded the greatest number of transfers with mismatched ownership records between 2015 and 2025, followed by Queens Village.

Neighborhoods with the greatest numbers of high-risk properties and flagged transfers tended to have larger shares of Black, Asian, and foreign-born residents than the city overall.

The Furman Center has also developed a restricted mapping tool to help government agencies, law enforcement, and legal services providers identify properties that may need intervention.

Researchers say more detailed property records, targeted legal assistance, and estate planning could help protect homeowners before ownership disputes or fraudulent transactions put their homes at risk.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5545. AI’s future starts to look surprisingly old-school: theCUBE’s KubeCon day one keynote analysis

The cloud-native community that turned Kubernetes into an enterprise standard is now being asked to carry artificial intelligence into production. As the underlying technology looks more alike from one company to the next, the hunt for domain-specific AI value is spotlighting how AI is put to work – and how to do so safely.

That shift is on display this week in Salt Lake City, where the Cloud Native Computing Foundation has added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to its flagship conference. The plumbing built for microservices is proving to be the substrate for AI factories and agents, along with a renewed focus on tried-and-tested security and business principles, according to John Furrier (pictured, left), co-founder and executive analyst of theCUBE Research.

“The AI-native world that we’ve been covering and following and living — AI factories, the rise of agentic, which involves coding and now tasks — are all based fundamentally on the substrate of cloud-native technologies,” Furrier said. “This community is the heart and soul for the AI generation.”

Furrier spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight (right) as a part of a keynote analysis at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can secure and govern AI agents while turning proprietary knowledge and workflows into measurable business value rather than simply maximizing token consumption. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has matured from a niche orchestration project into the reference platform for major clouds and neoclouds, and enterprises are now standardizing on it. That maturity is what makes it useful for AI, which needs the same control planes, scalable data layers and telemetry the community already worked out for microservices, according to Furrier.

“Kubernetes got boring, which means it’s working,” Furrier said. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world.”

Those lessons now apply to a pressing question: how much freedom enterprises will give AI agents inside real systems. Agents that cause trouble are usually poorly instructed rather than malicious, and the answer lies in context, identity and guardrails, according to Furrier. Perimeter-style security thinking is expected to make a comeback, along with a move away from token consumption as a measure of value and toward tangible business outcomes.

“We’re gonna get back to an era of, ‘Build something, show me what you built, present it for value,'” Furrier said. “If it’s worth something, there’s an exchange for value.”
